- list 1 of 3Seoul court orders North Korea to pay $32.5m for blowing up office
- list 2 of 3South Korea says US-North Korea talks possible, rules out Hormuz deployment
- list 3 of 3North Korea anthem played at South’s Bangladesh hockey match at Asian Games
In a separate statement to KCNA, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, accused the nuclear watchdog of double standards.
The IAEA’s “biased viewpoint and double standards” are “the fundamental factor causing the collapse of the international nuclear non-proliferation system”, she said.
Kim Yo Jong said the UN nuclear watchdog had turned a blind eye to the “blatant nuclear proliferation activities” of the United States and South Korea’s “nuclear submarine introduction plan”, while the agency forcibly adopted a resolution against North Korea’s “self-defensive and legitimate nuclear activities”.
The North Korean Foreign Ministry also accused “hostile forces” of seeking to bring an end to the country’s nuclear programme during this week’s general conference of the IAEA.
“Pitifully, the ‘resolution’ cooked up by the US and the West has no effect on the DPRK’s position as a nuclear weapons state,” a foreign ministry spokesperson said, referring to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, its official name.
The state media also reported that Kim Jong Un carried out a three-day inspection tour of major munitions factories this week.
Analysts say North Korea has been overhauling its military with Russian help since the two countries signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024. They say combat experience gained by Pyongyang’s troops deployed to the war in Ukraine has also aided the effort.
Kim Jong Un also gave a lecture to a propaganda workers’ training session in Pyongyang on Friday, KCNA reported, telling attendees modern “ideological warfare” needed to be innovative, creative and aggressive rather than repeating old methods.
Trump’s overtures
While Kim Yo Jong rebuked what she called double standards favouring the US and South Korea, both countries have recently said they want to improve relations with North Korea.
On Friday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said that US President Donald Trump wants dialogue with Pyongyang, and Seoul will work to facilitate potential talks.
Trump, seeking to revive the bond he forged with Kim Jong Un in his first term, said last month that he plans to meet the North Korean leader later this year.
The US president said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Iran sends US ‘seven conditions’ for talks, warns nuclear doctrine could change
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has again raised the possibility of a major new military escalation against Iran while keeping the door open to negotiations, but Tehran is responding with demands of its own. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Saturday that Qatar had conveyed Tehran’s conditions to Washington and that Iran was awaiting Trump’s response, while warning that the country’s nuclear doctrine could eventually change.
Trump told Axios on Thursday that he was approaching a major decision over whether to restart large-scale attacks against Iran, asking whether he wanted to “go in and annihilate” the Iranian regime. At the same time, he has publicly said he remains open to diplomacy and has claimed Iran wants a deal. Tehran has disputed that negotiations have resumed and has insisted there will be no talks until its conditions are met.
Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran remained in contact with mediators in Qatar and Pakistan. He said the three conditions publicly presented for ending the war were an end to fighting “on all fronts,” the release of frozen Iranian assets and an end to the U.S. naval blockade. Reuters independently reported the same three demands.
Iranian reports have referred more broadly to seven conditions communicated to Washington through intermediaries, particularly in connection with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The complete official list has not been publicly released, though earlier Iranian statements have also demanded sanctions relief and an end to U.S. military pressure.
Rezaei argued that Washington would ultimately have to accept Tehran’s position and said Iran was prepared for what he called a “decisive war.” He also claimed Iran had identified vulnerabilities in the U.S. military and had recently tested an anti-ship missile near an American aircraft carrier. Those claims have not been independently verified.
Rezaei also sharpened Tehran’s nuclear warnings, saying U.S. and Israeli actions could provide grounds for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. He said no decision had yet been taken and that Tehran’s next steps would depend on Washington’s conduct.
Iran, he said, remained committed to the religious ruling issued by Ali Khamenei prohibiting nuclear weapons and had not changed its declared nuclear doctrine. But he added that Tehran could not say what would happen in the future, leaving open the possibility of a later shift.
The warning comes amid a renewed confrontation between Tehran and the International Atomic Energy Agency. The IAEA’s Board of Governors this month referred Iran’s nuclear noncompliance to the UN Security Council, saying the agency still lacked access to key sites and information about nuclear material following the attacks on Iranian facilities. Tehran has blamed the U.S. and Israel for creating the situation and continues to say its nuclear program is not intended to produce weapons.
The nuclear and diplomatic standoff is unfolding alongside a major escalation in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis have made rapid gains against forces aligned with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and supported by Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have seized strategic positions along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. Their advances have increased their ability to threaten shipping at the western entrance to the Red Sea at the same time that the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted by the Iran conflict.
Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran wanted the Saudi-Houthi fighting to end and said he believed the Houthis were also interested in an agreement with Riyadh. Iran provides extensive support to the group but maintains that the Houthis make their own decisions.
The fighting has meanwhile moved deeper into Saudi territory. On Saturday, the Houthis said they had attacked “sensitive” sites in Riyadh with missiles and drones after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the Saudi capital’s main airport. They also claimed an attack on an Aramco facility in Yanbu, a crucial Red Sea oil export hub. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm what had been struck in Riyadh.
Yanbu has become particularly important because Saudi Arabia has relied on its Red Sea export infrastructure to bypass disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. But Saudi energy routes have themselves come under growing pressure, including attacks on the kingdom’s East-West pipeline and other infrastructure.
The Houthi offensive has also exposed growing unease in Washington and Gulf capitals about whether Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies can reverse the group’s advances.
Multiple U.S. and Gulf sources told CNN that neither Washington nor Riyadh currently has a clear plan for pushing the Houthis back. U.S. intelligence and targeting assistance has increased, but sources expressed doubt that Saudi Arabia could stop the Houthis without additional support.
Former U.S. diplomat Joey Hood told CNN that the Houthi advance in the Red Sea was strengthening the position of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and complicating any effort to negotiate separately with Tehran. Other regional officials argued that the Yemen front can no longer easily be separated from the wider confrontation with Iran.
A Gulf official summed up the dilemma to CNN: “No one wants to fight alone.” The official said Riyadh would ultimately have to either expand its military campaign or pursue an agreement with the Houthis.
Trump has so far resisted direct U.S. offensive action against the Houthis. CNN reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump for U.S. strikes but that the request was rejected, while American assistance has remained focused on intelligence and targeting support. The Washington Post similarly reported that Washington has stopped short of military intervention despite Saudi and Yemeni appeals.
U.S. officials also met Houthi representatives in Oman this month, according to Reuters. Sources said the Houthis reiterated their commitment to the 2025 ceasefire with Washington and said they did not intend to attack American vessels. One Yemeni source said they also pledged not to target Israeli or other commercial vessels, with the exception of Saudi ships. The State Department did not formally confirm the meeting.
The widening regional conflict has also intensified economic pressure in the United States. Oil prices have remained around or above $100 a barrel, while higher gasoline and diesel costs have become an increasingly prominent political issue ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump has publicly insisted that electoral politics do not determine his Iran policy and has defended higher energy costs as a price worth paying to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Privately, however, The Washington Post reported Saturday that Trump has listened more closely in recent weeks as advisers presented discouraging polling and has indicated in some conversations that he understands the Iran war has contributed to the difficult political environment facing Republicans. One person in frequent contact with Trump disputed that he had accepted responsibility, saying the president instead believes the biggest problem is that his own name will not be on the ballot.
The Post reported that advisers have become more direct with Trump about the political environment and that he intends to increase his involvement in Republican campaigns as the midterms approach. The extent to which the Iran war, oil prices and the widening confrontation in Yemen ultimately shape voter decisions remains uncertain.

articles.title: US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortages –  Bloomberg
articles.body:
US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortages – Bloomberg
The US has warned allies to expect delays of up to five years in the delivery of key types of weaponry, as the country works to replenish its own stockpiles, which have been depleted.
Source: Bloomberg, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to officials, a number of European countries expect deliveries of key missile systems and air defence assets to be delayed as a result of the US armed forces depleting their own arsenal during the war with Iran.
It is reported that Germany has asked the US to speed up the delivery of long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon ground-based launchers, but the depleted US stockpiles of this powerful weaponry mean its manufacturer, Raytheon, is unlikely to be able to fulfil the order within the next five years.
Two further officials said some Eastern European countries, which also rely on American weapons systems, had already encountered delays shortly after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February.
The Pentagon's decision to prioritise its own stockpiles is also complicating Ukraine's efforts to get the US to send it more Patriot interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a harsh winter.
The question of the air defence system Ukraine urgently needs will be a key topic at United Nations meetings taking place in New York next week.
It is estimated that the US used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missiles, a third of its Tomahawk missiles, and nearly half of its precision-strike missiles and THAAD interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said that, since June 2025, the US has likely used as much as two-thirds of its missile defence interceptor stockpiles.
The shortage of stockpiles is affecting not only the US and Europe. In April, the US told Japan that Tomahawk missile deliveries will be delayed by up to two years. Saudi Arabia has also called on allies, including the US, to provide military support to repel Houthi attacks in Yemen. Washington has not said whether it will provide additional assistance.
However, according to sources, the US is continuing to supply weapons purchased by European allies for Ukraine as part of NATO and European Union initiatives.
Background:
- CNN reported earlier that the United States has used around 80% of its available stockpiles for a key air defence system, with military officials warning that its warehouse levels are "dangerously low".
- Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth denied media reports that the US armed forces are running low on stockpiles of key missiles.
- US President Donald Trump threatened media sources with "long-term jail sentences" over the reports on US military ammunition shortages.
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Live: Russian strike on apartment building in Ukraine's Sumy kills at least two
articles.body:
Russia said Saturday that its electronic voting system in Moscow had come under “powerful” cyberattacks overnight, as parliamentary elections entered their second day. Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of seeking to “hinder” the vote, a claim Kyiv has not publicly addressed. Read about the day’s events as they unfolded on our liveblog.
Ukraine, Russia, hard to reconcile on Black Sea, Turkish FM says
Ukraine and Russian have positions on the Black Sea that are "difficult to reconcile" to end the attacks there, Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday in a television interview.
Exasperated by the ongoing Black Sea attacks, Turkey sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end strikes on civilian ships, a Turkish diplomat told AFP on Thursday.
"We sent proposals to both sides," Fidan told NTV. "We received responses from both sides.
"We are trying to reach a conclusion. Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile," he added.
"Our first priority is the extraction of grain from the Black Sea," said Fidan.
"Countries around the world need it. Grain is a product that both country sells. But there are difficulties to overcome.
Turkey's diplomatic initiative follows a sharp increase in attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea in recent months, often by drones, with many Turkish vessels among those targeted.
Elections with ‘no surprises’
Russians are voting to elect members of the Duma in what Alexander Titov, lecturer of modern European history at Queen’s University Belfast, calls an “unusual election”.
The Kremlin does not want to have “any surprises”, notes Titov. President Vladimir Putin “wants to show that elections can take place during wartime” in a pointed jab at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, “who says elections can’t be held during wartime", he explains.
Russian election observer loses consciousness during arrest by police, opposition party says
Russia’s liberal opposition Yabloko party has said that one of its election observers lost consciousness while being arrested by police at a St. Petersburg polling station on Saturday.
Yabloko said that officials at the polling station accused a party election observer of attempting to “disrupt the elections” and called the police, which “used force” against him.
It was unclear whether he received prompt medical attention after falling unconscious, the party said in a statement on Telegram Saturday, adding that he was taken to a police station and charged with disobeying police orders.
Russian officials didn't immediately comment on the incident.
Yabloko, the only registered political entity that dared to criticize Russia's war with Ukraine, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court, and only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races.
Russia cannot sway French through 'intimidation', Le Pen says
French policies will not be influenced by Russian "intimidation", far-right leader Marine Le Pen and her party's chief Jordan Bardella has said as they positioned themselves ahead of elections next year.
The two politicians from the National Rally (RN) party -- seen in the past as friendly towards Moscow -- condemned Russia's "hostile" acts against France.
Voter surveys put Le Pen as the front-runner in the first round of France's presidential election to take place in April next year, despite an appeals court upholding a graft conviction against her. Bardella is expected to become her prime minister if she ends up winning.
Their joint statement putting distance between themselves and Moscow came after the Kremlin this week ordered Russian subsidiaries of several big French businesses seized, along with the subsidiary of Swiss food giant Nestle.
Moscow said the move was a blow against "unfriendly countries" that back Ukraine, which it has invaded and is fighting to conquer.
French President Emmanuel Macron -- who is not contesting next year's election, having reached his two-term limit -- on Friday hosted a meeting of French political leaders to discuss the growing threat from Moscow. Le Pen did not attend the meeting.
Moldova suspects drone in 'unacceptable' airspace violation
Moldova has said it suspected a drone was behind an "unacceptable" violation of its airspace on Friday that resulted in an explosion near its capital Chisinau.
The incident, which caused no reported casualties or damage, "represents a new and serious consequence from Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine", Moldova's foreign ministry said in a statement.
It added that "any unauthorised entry into Moldovan airspace is unacceptable and constitutes a serious violation to our country's sovereignty".
The explosion occurred Friday in Colonita, a village close to Chisinau. Police said in a Facebook post they found debris apparently from a drone near the blast site. Authorities did not give the origin of the suspected drone.
Several drone incursions have been reported with increasing frequency in recent months in eastern European countries that have been attributed to the ongoing war in Ukraine launched by Russia in 2022.
Ukrainian children learn ancient warrior skills amid modern war
Ukrainian children are learning the skills of 17th-century Cossack warriors – the communities known for their military skills and horsemanship that played a central role in Ukraine history. But for these students, it is more than a history lesson. It is a chance to escape the reality of growing up during war.
France’s Macron warns of Russian ‘hybrid’ attacks, seeks to step up energy defence
Russia reports cyberattacks on second day of parliamentary vote
Russia said that its electronic voting system in Moscow had been hit by "powerful" cyberattacks overnight, as tightly controlled parliamentary elections entered a second day.
Ella Pamfilova, chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, did not give details on the nature of the attack or who was responsible.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of trying to "hinder" the vote, an accusation to which Kyiv has not responded. Ukraine has called the election farcical.
Poland concludes air operation with no airspace violations recorded
Poland has concluded the preventive military aviation operations that it started earlier on Saturday amid Russian strikes on Ukraine, the Polish army said in a post on X.
Ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance were returned to standard operational activities after the army activated them for a state of readiness, it added.
There was no violation of Polish airspace, the army said.
Russia hits Ukrainian cargo ship, tanker in Black Sea and Ukrainian port, Interfax says
Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo ship and a tanker located in the Black Sea and in one of Ukraine's ports, the Interfax news agency reported on Saturday, citing the Russian Defence Ministry.
FRANCE 24 could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Poland starts preventive military aviation operations as Russia strikes Ukraine, army says
Poland has started preventive military aviation operations to protect its airspace on Saturday amid Russian strikes on Ukraine, the Polish army said in a post on X.
The military has activated a state of readiness for ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance systems, it added.
US State Dept approves $2.7 billion sale to Ukraine for air-defence development upgrades
The United States approved a potential $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine on Friday, after Kyiv made repeated pleas for support to fend off Russian attacks.
The State Department said in a congressional notification that it made "a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine" for buying air defense development upgrades and related equipment and services.
Kyiv has requested to buy equipment including multiple types of missiles, launchers, counter-drone radars and trailers, according to the State Department.
The proposed sale is subject to congressional review.
"If the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior Administration," the State Department said.
"The estimated total cost is $2.68 billion."
Russia holds parliamentary vote in areas it seized from Ukraine in the war
Putin stressed the importance of voting in the regions.
Russia’s parliamentary election for the first time includes residents of regions that Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine after the start of its full-scale invasion more than 4 1/2 years ago, part of Kremlin efforts to cement its gains.
Officials in Kyiv vigorously denounced the action as illegal, and a human rights activist described residents there as being coerced to participate in the election.
Russian glide bomb hits apartment in Ukraine's Sumy, killing at least two and injuring seven
A Russian glide bomb hit an apartment building in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Friday, killing two people and injuring seven, three of them in serious condition, Regional Governor Oleh Hryhorov said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky denounced the "absolutely inhuman strike" on the apartment block and said residents could still be under rubble. He said Russian forces had also hit a clinic in the central city of Pavlohrad and a logistics centre outside Kyiv, but provided no details on casualties.
A morning Russian drone attack has injured five people, including three children, in the Kyiv region around the Ukrainian capital
The European Union slammed Russia's tightly controlled parliamentary elections on Friday, accusing the Kremlin of using repression to deprive voters of "a genuine choice about the future of their country".
French President Emmanuel Macron said he had ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites from "Russian hybrid attacks".

articles.title: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
articles.body:
In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale.
The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague.
This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it.
“You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement.
“The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that.
“[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there. It could just be a building block, and the US is going to lay out more later with that. To me that would make logical sense, if that was the plan.”
What the plan actually is has never been made clear, and Meink, in his announcement, stressed it was unlikely ever to be.
“Me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else,” he said.
But as Russia and China, both US adversaries, have advanced their own aggressive outer space ambitions and agendas, Trump has responded by placing an ever-increasing focus on militarizing the heavens.
During his first term of office, he created Space Force, the first new, separate branch of the US military in more than seven decades. Last month, he signed an executive order designating the first US Space Academy, a proposed joint civilian-military institution modeled on the army and navy training academies at West Point and Annapolis, to be sited at an as-yet unnamed location.
This week, Military Times reported plans to recruit and train 10,000 new guardians, as Space Force service members are known, to join uniformed ranks within the next five years.
Gen Dan Caine, who as chair of the joint chiefs of staff is the country’s most senior military leader, told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland this week, that the armed forces including Space Force must be “prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”.
Added to a number of other maneuvers and bold pronouncements Trump has made concerning space in recent weeks and months, it is hard not to see the space weapons reveal by Meink – who holds a civilian position reporting to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – as a further blending of the traditionally separate military and non-military roles of US space policy.
In August, the White House unveiled a national space transportation policy that gives Hegseth, as head of the defense department, new responsibility and authority to determine with the chief of Nasa, Jared Isaacman, who manages all US space launches, and sets an ambitious, expansive federal target of more than 1,000 launch and reentry operations by 2030.
The president, meanwhile, has made no secret of his desire for US astronauts to beat China and land on the moon before he leaves office in January 2029; and in March laid out plans, arguably rooted more in optimism than expectation, to invest $20bn (£15bn) on a moonbase to secure for the US the first permanent foothold on the lunar surface.
Some analysts see an almost sea change in the way the Trump administration has approached space in pursuit of its geopolitical goals, compared to previous presidents who upheld decades of separation between the government’s civilian and military needs.
“The way that the US has structured it since Nasa was established in the late 1950s was we have a civil space organization focused on civil exploration, on science, and then we have the Pentagon,” Swope said.
He continued: “There seems to be a tendency to pull them together more than we’ve seen in the past [and] the creation of the Space Academy is just another data point that suggests that at least within the eyes of this administration, the missions are very not just complementary, but very, very similar.
“The civilian space agency and Pentagon, [it’s] not just that they complement each other, but that they’re essentially doing the same mission.”
Certainly, Trump has become more visible in space circles since inviting Isaacman, at the second time of asking, to lead Nasa. Seen as an ally of Elon Musk, the billionaire SpaceX chief and former political acolyte of the president, Isaacman has proven a staunch Trump loyalist in social media posts and in public appearances.
It was the “experience of a lifetime”, Isaacman gushed on X, to accompany Trump on Air Force One to the Johnson Space Center in Houston last month, where the academy announcement was staged before rows of Nasa’s civilian astronaut corps bedecked in their blue flight suits.
In a separate, lengthier post, Isaacman defended the need for a space academy with military theming, arguing that US ambitions necessitated “a bright new generation educated and prepared for this environment”.
He wrote: “If you understand the increasingly important and contested environment above us, then [the academy] is as timely and necessary today as the Space Force has already proven to be.”
The argument that the academy blurs the line between peaceful applications in space and the military, he said, “may be the weakest argument I have seen”, before chronicling a succession of previous Nasa missions and operations that were classified and defense department-based, and noting the agency’s early rockets were modified and evolved from military ballistic missiles.
“Nasa’s mission is as peaceful as it is patriotic,” he said. “We explore for the benefit of all humankind, but we go there under our flag. That mission would be impossible without the Guardians standing watch over the domain as we venture outward.”
Lori Garver, a former deputy administrator of Nasa during the Biden administration, said that while she saw the academy as potentially helpful to the US space program and its future workforce, she was concerned it conflated the agency’s mission for peaceful, civil space exploration with Space Force’s military goals.
“Nasa’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” she told the science publication Ars Technica. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.”
Others say it is difficult, or impossible, for the US to remain committed to the 1967 Outer Space treaty that mandated, among other regulations, that all nations use space for peaceful, non-militarized ends when some countries are blatantly defying it.
US intelligence agencies said in 2024 they were monitoring the development of a new Russian space weapon with the capability of shooting down satellites in Earth’s orbit. Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the Space Force combat forces command, told reporters at the Maryland conference that China was “actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space”, which the country has denied.
A Space Force “threat fact sheet” details how Russia and China are both “testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities with the intent to disrupt and degrade US space-enabled capabilities”.
So, to Swope, the CSIS analyst who worked for the Central Intelligence Agency’s directorate of science and technology for more than a decade, the US’s declaration that it had deployed space weapons of its own was more significant than the absence of detail.
“It’s this idea of space superiority, ‘I want to use space, I don’t want my adversary to’,” he said. “That’s just where we are today.
“Is more of that happening in space? I don’t think this announcement is determining that, or even accelerating that. It may be more just a recognition that the US has woken up to it, and we may just not know it because it’s not public.”
Another question, he said, is what kind of weapons the US may have. “It has talked previously about systems that operate in the electromagnetic spectrum, for jamming or interference with radio signals, that’s what we know publicly about what is in the US counter-space arsenal,” he said.
“War is really bad whether it is confined to Earth or orbit, and maybe we need to have a better thought not just on how we could limit specific types of weapons, but that we want to avoid generally.
“You can’t just walk into a quote-unquote space war and expect that not to be ugly.”

articles.title: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict
articles.body:
As he stood in Riyadh last September, the world looked like a very different place for Pakistan’s most powerful man, Gen Asim Munir.
The country’s army chief was there to witness the signing of a historic defence pact with Saudi Arabia, which he had personally orchestrated with the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman.
To Munir, it appeared to be a highly strategic win: Riyadh would provide cash-strapped Pakistan with billions of dollars of life-saving investments and loans. In exchange, Pakistan agreed to train up the Saudi military, and Pakistan’s armed forces would defend Saudi Arabia in the unlikely event of an attack on its territory.
Analysts say it was clear that Pakistan presumed US-Iran relations would soon get back on track and the risk of a conflict sweeping across the Middle East and the Gulf was low.
But a very different scenario soon unfolded. By February, the Middle East was on fire after the US and Israel began bombing Iran – and Iran began firing missiles at the Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, in retaliation.
It did not take long for the war to reinflame Saudi’s conflict with the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel group based in Yemen, and for their fragile truce to collapse. Earlier this month the Houthis made unprecedented territorial gains in Yemen and hit Saudi territory with strikes and drones. Saudi Arabia has responded by pounding Yemen with airstrikes. Some believe a return to full-scale war is on the horizon.
The pressure is now mounting on Pakistan, and particularly Munir. In August, the defence pact with Saudi Arabia was extended to include Turkey and renamed the Mecca joint defence agreement. The countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a defence analyst and senior fellow at King’s College London, said: “I don’t think Asim Munir properly calculated the threats the region was facing – and that Pakistan might need to put its troops on the line quite so soon.”
Saudi Arabia has tens of billions of dollars in fighter jets and war machinery, but it does not have any warfare experience to fight the Houthis, who have proved to be tough, resilient fighters. Pakistan’s forces, trained to deal with the constant menace of India, would be highly valuable on the frontline.
Analysts say that if Saudi Arabia decided to activate the Mecca pact to fight the Houthis, Pakistan would have no choice but to send in its troops, including thousands who are already deployed in Saudi Arabia for training. As well as being a defence partner, Pakistan is almost totally economically and geopolitically dependent on Saudi Arabia, which has recently given the country a lifesaving $8bn (£6bn) in funds and investments.
Last week, Pakistani government ministers and senior military figures gave increasingly bullish statements, confirming their “unconditional” commitment to the pact and saying Islamabad would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia.
But privately, officials in Pakistan are deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. The country is already economically crippled, in a de facto war with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and facing an uncontrollable surge in militancy in its border areas.
To many, an activation of the Mecca pact would be perceived as Islamabad taking a clear stance against Iran. Before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Pakistan had good relations with its neighbour – ties that Munir utilised to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in his attempt to secure a lasting ceasefire. But as the war has dragged on, Pakistan has become increasingly infuriated with Iran, while Tehran has little trust left in Islamabad.
As Siddiqa emphasised, Pakistan joining the fight against the Houthis “would come with major repercussions”. After Iran, Pakistan is home to the second-largest population of Shia Muslims, who would probably rise up in protest against any involvement in strikes on the Houthis.
Iran also maintains good relations with the Taliban in Afghanistan, posing the risk of further provoking one of Pakistan’s biggest security threats and driving militancy and security problems along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border to even deadlier levels.
It also risks inflaming the situation in Balochistan, Pakistan’s unstable border region with Iran, which is home to a long-running and uncontrollable insurgency.
Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in Pakistan’s senate, said that only the very few at the top of Pakistan’s military even knew what conditions and agreements had been made in the Mecca pact. With the military as Pakistan’s de facto rulers, the decision to join was not even put before parliament.
“It will be a disaster for the country if Pakistan jumps into war,” said Abbas. “We are already facing two lethal insurgencies; our economy is in a shambles and inflation has rocketed. If we take Saudi Arabia’s side in this conflict, the country will face chaos, instability and religious division.”
So far, no one has been able to pinpoint what the “red line” would be that would force the pact to be activated. Analysts said Pakistan appeared to be banking on Riyadh’s reluctance to enter into open warfare with Iran by escalating its fight with the Houthis. Turkey has also made it clear it does not want to enter the fray.
“Pakistan will do its best not to get involved in any incursion on Yemeni soil,” said Muhammad Amir Rana, the director of the Islamabad-based Pak Institute for Peace Studies.
Speaking privately, one senior official said he did not think the Saudi crown prince “wants to activate the pact now”.
“If the kingdom plans to send its ground forces, Pakistan would support that,” he said. “But I don’t think Saudi Arabia would start a full-fledged war against the Houthis without American approval and Trump has snubbed them. Right now, the US does not want to open up another front; they prefer talking to Houthis.”
He added: “You can’t predict the future though.”

articles.title: North Korea reveals new drone production lines
articles.body:
- North Korean state media showed Kim Jong Un touring drone production lines Sept. 16-18, including a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions.
- The drone's launcher system first appeared publicly at an October 2025 military parade, mounted six per truck on four vehicles.
North Korean state media revealed production lines for at least three types of domestically built drones this week, including a one-way attack drone that resembles Israeli-designed loitering munitions, as part of a factory tour by leader Kim Jong Un reported Sept. 19.
The ruling Workers’ Party newspaper Rodong Sinmun said Kim, the party’s general secretary, inspected “important munitions industry enterprises” from Sept. 16 to 18. Photos accompanying the report showed him walking through an assembly hall containing dozens of small flying-wing drones mounted on stands, alongside separate images of him examining what appeared to be missile or drone airframe components with factory officials.
One drone shown is a one-way attack type visually similar to Israel’s Harop family of loitering munitions, weapons built to fly toward a target and detonate on impact rather than return to base. North Korea unveiled a dedicated launch system for this drone at a nighttime military parade on Oct. 10, 2025, marking the Workers’ Party’s 80th anniversary.
That parade featured four 6×6 trucks, each carrying two stacked rows of three launch containers, for an apparent capacity of six drones per vehicle. The parade followed an August 2024 reveal of prototype airframes styled after Israel’s Harop and Switchblade-style “Hero” loitering munitions, neither of which came with published performance figures at the time.
This week’s images of the attack drone during testing were partly obscured, withholding a clear view of some components, though analysts have suggested the design may be related to a rail-launched drone North Korea has separately tested that uses a small rocket booster to get airborne.
Other drones shown on the factory floor were still semi-complete airframes, but their shape already matched North Korea’s larger reconnaissance-strike drones, the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9.
Both first appeared publicly in July 2023 and have undergone repeated flight tests since. The Saetbyol-4 bears a resemblance to the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk surveillance drone, while the Saetbyol-9, with a wingspan of roughly 20 meters (66 feet), resembles the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper and carries hardpoints that suggest it is built to fire guided weapons rather than only observe. North Korean state media has separately called for expanded production across the country’s drone programs, following Kim’s public push earlier this year to accelerate output.
The factory visit came the same week Kim toured facilities producing a mobile rocket launcher that outside analysts have compared to the U.S. Army’s HIMARS system, and the same week North Korea rejected an International Atomic Energy Agency resolution criticizing its nuclear weapons program.
North Korea has not disclosed the factory locations, production quantities for any of the drones shown, or further technical detail on the attack drone beyond what appears in the partly obscured photos.

articles.title: US approves possible F-35 Saudi deal despite Israeli push to link normalization, sale - analysis
articles.body:
The US State Department’s announcement on Thursday that it is advancing the sale of 48 F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia represents far more than a massive arms deal worth $24.3 billion. For Israel, it highlights a concerning diplomatic shift: one of Washington’s most valuable security leverage tools with Riyadh is now moving forward on its own track, without Saudi Arabia first being required to normalize relations with Israel.
The State Department approved the possible sale of 48 F-35A Lightning II aircraft, alongside 49 Pratt & Whitney F135 engines, communications and encryption systems, electronic warfare capabilities, simulators, training, spare parts and logistical support.
The move does not yet constitute a final contract. The announcement is a stage in the US arms sale process, and a legally required review period in Congress has now begun. In Saudi Arabia’s case, the official review period is 30 days.
The administration is presenting the deal as part of efforts to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ability to confront current and future threats and deepen its joint operational capabilities with the United States and regional partners. The official announcement explicitly stated that the deal “will not alter the military balance in the region.”
In the United States, Israel’s qualitative military edge is enshrined in law. The statement touches on the core of Israel’s concern: Israel is currently the only country in the Middle East operating the F-35, in its Israeli configuration, the F-35I “Adir.”
US law requires the administration to ensure that arms sales to other countries in the region do not harm Israel’s “Qualitative Military Edge,” meaning its qualitative military advantage. The requirement was codified in legislation in 2008 and requires significant regional arms deals to be examined through the Israeli security lens as well.
The political price Israel sought for the F-35 deal
The Trump administration approved the sale of advanced F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia. Israel sought a diplomatic price.
However, Jerusalem’s concern is not only technical or related to air capabilities. In November 2025, Israeli officials said that Israel did not fundamentally oppose Saudi Arabia receiving F-35 aircraft, provided the deal was part of full normalization between Riyadh and Jerusalem.
“We told the Trump administration that supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia should be contingent on Saudi normalization with Israel,” an Israeli official said at the time.
Another Israeli official warned that providing the aircraft to Riyadh without receiving diplomatic concessions would be a “mistake” and a move that would work against US interests.
That link did not materialize. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said during his visit to the White House last year that he was interested in Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, but conditioned progress on the creation of a “clear path” toward a two-state solution.
The gap between Riyadh and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government on the Palestinian issue has remained. Despite that, the F-35 track continued to advance.
This is the central difference between the deal Israel hoped to see and the deal as it currently appears: Jerusalem wanted the stealth aircraft as part of a broader regional strategic package centered on normalization. Washington, at least at this stage, is not waiting for such an agreement before moving ahead.
China concerns surrounding the Saudi F-35 sale
Jonathan Ruhe, a specialist in US strategy at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA), told Walla that in his view, the F-35 deal should not move forward in its current form before two central issues are resolved.
The concern is not merely theoretical. The New York Times reported two days ago that US intelligence officials warned in internal assessments that China could obtain F-35-related technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through its security and technology ties with the kingdom.
One report by the Pentagon’s intelligence agency addressed, among other issues, Chinese access to Saudi bases and Saudi use of Chinese communications infrastructure. Reports on Thursday’s deal also noted that expanding security ties between Riyadh and Beijing are among the concerns surrounding the sale.
Ruhe’s second concern directly relates to Israel.
“The entire F-35 program is intended to support US-led collective defense,” he said. “America needs to demonstrate leadership in integrating Saudi Arabia into a new regional security architecture, and Riyadh also needs to show that it is a committed partner before it can receive F-35 aircraft.”
According to Ruhe, Israel’s qualitative military edge must remain part of the equation.
“Israel’s QME is a central factor in this regional integration, and it needs to be reflected in any possible F-35 deal with the kingdom,” he said.
Ruhe added that the United States has significant leverage in the matter.
“The United States has leverage here, because it can offer Saudi Arabia much more than China can,” he said.
Even if the deal is completed, a significant question remains over the exact capabilities that will be transferred to Riyadh.
The aircraft intended for Saudi Arabia are expected to be less advanced in several areas than Israel’s F-35I aircraft, partly as part of the US effort to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge. Israel also benefits from the ability to integrate unique Israeli systems into its aircraft.
The issue became more complicated after US President Donald Trump publicly said that Saudi Arabia would receive advanced aircraft similar to Israel’s. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reassured Netanyahu and told him that Saudi Arabia would receive a downgraded version and that the United States remained committed to preserving Israel’s qualitative military edge.
Therefore, even after the State Department announcement and assurances regarding reduced capabilities for Saudi Arabia, key details remain undisclosed: which capabilities will be included in the aircraft, what restrictions will be placed on their deployment and access, and what Israel will receive to ensure that its advantage is maintained.
But on the diplomatic level, a significant development has already taken place: the F-35, which Israel wanted to see as part of the price Saudi Arabia would pay for joining the Abraham Accords, is moving toward Riyadh even as normalization itself remains stalled.

articles.title: RM-48U Missiles Make Up More Than Half of Ballistic and Hypersonic Missiles Fired at Ukraine in July and August
articles.body:
Russian RM-48U missiles accounted for more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August.
This information was reported by Reuters, which reviewed data from the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine.
In its standard configuration, the RM-48U is a target missile manufactured from decommissioned 5V55 or 48N6 anti-aircraft missiles used in the S-300PM and S-400 air defense systems.
In these training missiles, the warhead is replaced with measuring instruments or ballast, after which the RM-48U is used for exercises and to train air defense crews.
The use of RM-48U missiles against ground targets was first reported in January of this year.
To this end, they are equipped with a warhead weighing 199 kg. At the same time, the RM-48U can also be used to divert attention and deplete Ukrainian air defense missile stocks.
“The RM-48U flies along a ballistic trajectory at high speed, but it is less powerful and less accurate than the ‘Iskander,’” a representative from the prosecutor’s office told the publication.
The scale of the RM-48U deployment demonstrates how Russia managed to expand its attacks over the summer without depleting its stockpiles of Iskander missiles and other primary-purpose missiles.
As the number of attacks using the RM-48U increased in July, the number of Iskander missiles launched dropped to 38—down from over 100 the previous month.
In July, Russia launched the largest number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in a single month since the start of its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Of the 158 strikes, 87 were carried out with RM-48U missiles, the data shows.
The Ukrainian Prosecutor General’s Office has linked the RM-48U missile to several strikes that have caused a large number of civilian casualties over the past few months, including the strike on a train platform in the Brovary district.
“The RM-48U missiles deviate from their targets by an average of approximately 300 meters, and their explosive warheads can scatter metal fragments over a large area,” the prosecutor’s office stated.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that Russia plans to more than double production of RM-48U missiles—to 480 this year compared to 200 last year. It is known that these missiles contain foreign components.
Recently, in the Bryansk region, Ukrainian strikes destroyed two launchers of the S-400 system, which are capable of firing these missiles.

articles.title: Europe falls behind in drone warfare technology, vulnerable to Russian missile attacks — Latvian President
articles.body:
Europe falls behind in drone warfare technology, vulnerable to Russian missile attacks — Latvian President
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs issued the warning in an interview with The Guardian, as reported by Ukrinform.
The Latvian president said that drone warfare in Ukraine is developing at "lightning speed," while current efforts and preparations for aerial warfare could become outdated as early as the middle of next year.
"What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems. And let's be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and Nato has it," Rinkēvičs said.
He added that a sudden Russian air strike involving several launched missiles would, in his view, become a serious challenge that would be difficult to deal with for many countries today.
Ukraine and its European allies are currently facing delays in the delivery of critical missiles for Patriot systems and other air-defense capabilities.
The United States has considered transferring production of Patriot systems to Ukraine and European countries, but no agreement has yet been concluded.
Rinkēvičs said that the matter depended on the US government and the company itself, adding that negotiations were still ongoing and that there were certain technical difficulties related to licensing.
According to Rinkēvičs, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and recent incidents involving drones and missiles indicated that Russia was testing Europe's resolve to continue supporting Ukraine. He said that he did not consider a conventional military invasion likely, but stressed that Europe needed to remain very vigilant about other possible scenarios.
He also suggested that, in the coming months following the local elections, Russia could intensify its mobilization and then use the winter period to put pressure on the Ukrainian front and take every possible measure to discourage countries supporting Ukraine from providing further assistance.
As Ukrinform reported, on September 15, aircraft participating in NATO's air-policing mission shot down a Russian drone over Lithuania after it entered from the direction of Belarus. It was later discovered that the drone was a Russian Gerbera UAV that had deviated from its course.

Russia kills eight people in Ukraine, attacks two vessels in Black Sea
Ukraine’s Air Force says Russia hit the country with dozens of drones and two antiship missiles overnight.
Russian forces have launched widespread missile, drone, and artillery attacks across Ukraine, causing civilian casualties while hitting regional infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukraine’s Air Force on Saturday reported facing a huge overnight barrage involving 174 drones from across Russia and Ukraine’s annexed Crimean Peninsula, alongside two Zircon antiship missiles launched from Russia’s Kursk region.

The Air Force said in a statement on Telegram that air defences intercepted or jammed 141 incoming targets, with downings recorded in 15 locations and falling debris in nine others. “Enemy [Zircon antiship] missiles did not reach the targets,” it said.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed its forces used Geran-4 Seeker loitering drones to strike two commercial vessels in the Black Sea – a Ukrainian dry cargo ship en route to Odesa and a docked tanker in the port of Odesa – asserting that both ships were carrying military supplies.

In the Kherson region, shelling across 25 communities killed three people and injured five others, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin. The bombardment also damaged high-rise apartments, private homes, a cell tower, and a gas pipeline, he said.
The Dnipropetrovsk region came under heavy fire, enduring more than 10 separate Russian attacks across four areas using drones, artillery, and aerial bombs, head of the regional administration Oleksandr Ganzha said.
“Two people were injured. The enemy attacked four areas more than 10 times with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs.”
The attacks damaged local warehouses in Dnipro, an outpatient clinic in Pavlohrad, a shopping centre in Nikopol, and several homes across Kryvyi Rih and Synelnyky.
Poland on high alert
Meanwhile, Poland scrambled fighter jets and placed its air defence systems on high readiness as Russia launched a wide-scale aerial attack across neighbouring Ukraine.
The Polish military’s Operational Command said in a statement on X on Saturday that it had launched military flights inside national airspace, citing heavy Russian drone activity nearby.
“In connection with strikes carried out by the Russian Federation using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles on the territory of Ukraine, military aviation operations have begun in Polish airspace,” the Polish Operational Command said.
It further said it had “activated all necessary forces and resources at its disposal”, and that “ground-based air defence and radar reconnaissance systems have reached the highest state of readiness.”
The brief operation concluded shortly after, with ground-based air defence and radar units returning to standard duty, the command said in a follow-up statement.
Confirming that no airspace violations occurred, it said the armed forces remained on alert and continued to monitor the situation across the border to secure Polish airspace.

articles.title: Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis and that Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan.
"We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity and sovereignty. We have an alliance agreement in our pact. We are in serious solidarity on this point... They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these," Fidan told broadcaster NTV.
The joint defence agreement, dubbed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, have been launching attacks on Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, threatening global oil supplies and the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
US President Donald Trump has rebuffed pleas from the Saudis for military support to fight the Houthis, who agreed a ceasefire with the United States last year after Washington bombed the group for two months.
Fidan said that it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war as it had no desire to join the conflict. He added, without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting.
"There are many initiatives, but the sides need to accept these," he said. "There are new proposals, I hope they accept them. Otherwise, the crisis was tolerated until a certain point, but the economic reflections have started to exceed the point of being tolerable."
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
Pakistan has said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan would act when the "time comes".
Earlier on Saturday, Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.
Turkey has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately.

articles.title: French channel apologizes after depicting nuclear strike on Tel Aviv
articles.body:
French television channel RMC Découverte publicly apologized and removed a documentary about the future of French weaponry from all its platforms after it emerged that a 3D simulation used to illustrate a future nuclear strike actually depicted Tel Aviv as the target.
The documentary, “Nouveau Rafale, drones et canons: la révolution dans l'armement français” — “New Rafale, Drones and Cannons: The Revolution in French Weaponry” — aired Sept. 1 and examined the next generation of French weapons systems, including the Rafale F5 fighter jet and the future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear missile, which is designed to be launched from the aircraft.
The missile, which reports say could be 10 to 20 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb and have a range of more than 1,000 kilometers, does not yet exist operationally. According to the Brussels Signal website, France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, commissioned its development in early June with the aim of introducing it into service around 2035.
To illustrate the weapon’s capabilities, the documentary used a 3D simulation showing a fighter jet launching a missile toward a coastal city, followed by a nuclear mushroom cloud rising above it.
According to Libération, French researcher Héloïse Fayet, who specializes in nuclear issues at the French Institute of International Relations, identified the city in the simulation as Tel Aviv rather than a fictional location and alerted the channel.
An independent Jewish-owned production company involved in making the documentary had taken the explosion footage from a video game, apparently without realizing the location depicted.
On Sept. 18, RMC Découverte posted a statement on X, rather than on its official website, saying it was “immediately removing the documentary from all its platforms” and “suspending any further broadcast.”
The channel explicitly acknowledged that the simulation “uses an image of Tel Aviv” in Israel rather than a fictional city and offered its “sincere apologies” to viewers.
According to the broadcaster, the clip “came from a professional image database, which incorrectly identified and cataloged it.”
The channel added that it would consider “any appropriate legal action against those responsible for the error” and said a corrected version of the documentary, without the disputed segment, would be released later.
The apology came about 17 days after the original broadcast, which was watched by about 241,000 viewers, according to figures published in France.
Israel’s ambassador to France, Joshua “Yosh” Zarka, brought wider attention to the incident when he shared the clip on X, describing it as “an animated demonstration of a French nuclear strike on Tel Aviv.” He also noted that the explosion shown was significantly less powerful than the yield attributed to the ASN4G missile.
Zarka said, however, that he did not believe there had been malicious intent behind the use of Tel Aviv in the simulation.
The film’s director, Alex Gary, said he was “deeply shocked” by the incident. He said the description accompanying the clip in the image database did not indicate at any point that it depicted a real city or a location in Israel and that, had he known, he would not have included the simulation.
By then, however, the footage had already circulated and was amplified by figures hostile to Israel.

articles.title: New images reveal severe destruction at US base in Kuwait
articles.body:
Several structures at the base appear to have been completely destroyed, with surrounding areas also heavily damaged, accoridng to a report by Press TV. Buildings that were once operational have been reduced to rubble, with debris scattered across the site.

The base’s airfield was also completely destroyed in the strike, according to the images.
The findings are consistent with separate reporting by ABC News this week, which published images and video showing extensive damage to buildings and at least one aircraft at three US bases in Kuwait, including Camp Arifjan, as well as at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.
Some US assets at the Saudi base were evacuated amid the danger. CBS News also reported on widespread damage to US bases earlier in the week.

ABC News reported that images obtained from US forces show damaged buildings and an aircraft at three bases in Kuwait and at a Saudi base hosting US assets.

A senior US troop described the extent of the damage as severe and said rebuilding the affected bases would be a decades-long undertaking. The troop also criticized the Pentagon for a lack of transparency over continuing drone and ballistic missile attacks on US bases.

Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile targeting the capital Riyadh early Saturday, according to the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki said in a statement on US social media platform X that the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces intercepted the missile after it was launched by Yemen’s Houthi group toward Riyadh.
Al-Maliki said the escalation “by the terrorist Houthi militia and its persistent attempts to target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital Riyadh – a city inhabited by over 8 million citizens and residents – demonstrates the militia's intransigence and its deliberate, systematic targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure, reflecting a hostile and terrorist pattern of behavior.”
He also said the group attempted to target civilians and civilian facilities in Baysh, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu, but that Saudi air defenses thwarted the attacks.
The coalition spokesman said the coalition leadership reserves the right to take measures it deems appropriate to deter Houthi attacks in line with international humanitarian law.
The Saudi statement came after Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed that the group had carried out two operations involving “a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones.”
Saree said one operation targeted what he described as “sensitive targets” in Riyadh, while another targeted Saudi Aramco oil company facilities in the coastal city of Yanbu.
Earlier Saturday, Saudi Civil Defense issued alerts in Riyadh for the first time during the latest wave of warnings, as well as in nearby Al-Kharj. Authorities did not initially specify the nature of the threat.
