articles.title: First new British warhead since the early nineties advances
articles.body:
The Astraea programme passed its System Design Review in August 2025, a step the Ministry of Defence describes as significant for the design, safety, performance assessment and manufacturability of what will be the first new British nuclear warhead since the early 1990s, according to the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament.
The government has committed £15 billion from 2025/26 to 2029/30 to the warhead programme, which includes development of Astraea.
The update states that Astraea “will be the first new UK warhead since the Mk4 warhead (subsequently upgraded to Mk4A) entered service in the early 1990s, and the first to be designed in the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) era without explosive nuclear testing”.
Designing a warhead without the ability to test it is the central technical challenge of the programme, and the update lists the capabilities delivery depends on, covering products and technology, advanced manufacturing, warhead physics, materials, mission effectiveness, hardness and vulnerability, scientific computing, radiation protection and regulatory science, and criticality safety and non-destructive assay.
AWE is to publish an updated warhead science, engineering and technology strategy this year, compliant with the test ban treaty.
The organisation designs, manufactures and maintains British nuclear warheads, was brought back into government ownership in 2021 and marked its 75th anniversary in 2025. The update says it is undergoing a transformation including major recapitalisation of its infrastructure and nationwide investment across its supply chain and its science, engineering and technology base.
The current warhead remains the Mk4A, fitted to Trident missiles and maintained by AWE at Aldermaston, with the design sovereign to Britain. AWE assures the effectiveness and performance of the warheads along with the safety and security of the stockpile.
The update describes delivery of Astraea as a national endeavour drawing on expertise across government, industry, academia and international partners, with sovereign capability enhanced by partnerships with the United States under the Mutual Defence Agreement and the Polaris Sales Agreement.
The Mutual Defence Agreement, extended indefinitely in 2024, enables cooperation between the two countries on atomic energy for mutual defence purposes, including the exchange of nuclear materials and technology, the transfer of non-nuclear components and collaborative scientific exchanges on technology and nuclear threat reduction.
The missiles the warhead sits on are American built, with Trident and its supporting systems manufactured in the United States, with Britain having bought title to a number drawn from a shared pool of assets under the 1963 Polaris Sales Agreement as amended for Trident in 1982, and the system is operated independently by both the Royal Navy and the United States Navy.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least 11 and injure dozens over past 24 hours
articles.body:
The Ukrainian air force reported that Russian forces had fired two “Zircon” missiles as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight.
Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 11 people and injured dozens more over the past day, according to local authorities.
In Kharkiv Oblast in northeastern Ukraine, five people were killed and 15 were injured in Russian attacks, governor Oleh Syniehubov reported, adding that Russian forces had fired two missiles, five guided aerial bombs, and almost 60 drones at targets across the region.
Strikes reportedly hit the villages of Lypkuvativka, Velykyi Burluk, and Slatyne, as well as the cities of Kharkiv and Balakliia, among other locations.
Two people were also killed and five were wounded following a wave of drone attacks, air strikes, and artillery shelling across the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, per the Kherson Regional State Administration.
"Russian troops struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging, in particular, five high-rise buildings and seven private homes," it said in a statement posted on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed administrative buildings, stores, a cell tower, a utility building, a gas pipeline, and private vehicles".
In Donetsk in the east of the country, one person was killed in the city of Kramatorsk while 13 people were injured across the wider region.
A 51-year-old man and a 45-year-old woman were also killed after a guided missile struck a high-rise building in Sumy Oblast in the north, authorities said. A 32-year-old man also died following a drone attack in the region.
The Sumy Regional Military Administration reported 50 attacks on 21 settlements from Friday to Saturday morning, with Russian forces said to have launched drones, mortars, artillery, and guided aerial bombs.
It comes as the Ukrainian air force reported that Russia had fired two “Zircon” missiles from its Kursk region as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight.
"According to preliminary data, as of 8 am, air defence forces shot down or neutralized 141 targets," the force said, adding that strikes had been recorded at 15 locations.
On Saturday, Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said it had activated air defence measures and scrambled military aircraft in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine.
"These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in regions adjacent to threatened areas," it said in a statement.

articles.title: Drones have reportedly appeared near UK Ministry of Defence sites almost daily over past year
articles.body:
Drones have reportedly appeared near UK Ministry of Defence sites almost daily over past year
The Independent has reported that unidentified drones have appeared near UK Ministry of Defence sites almost every day, leaving the country vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran.
Source: The Independent, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Independent said, citing data obtained under freedom of information laws, that around 340 drone-related incidents had been recorded at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026. A total of 250 incidents were recorded in 2025, twice the 126 reported the previous year.
Experts warned that the alarming increase highlights serious shortcomings in government security measures and a lack of preparedness to counter hostile threats amid escalating activity by Russia under Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and aggression from Iran.
The UK Ministry of Defence did not provide details of who it suspects was behind the incidents. Experts, however, said hostile actors working in the interests of Moscow or Tehran are the most obvious suspects. The figures, obtained under freedom of information laws, emerged as Poland warned that the Kremlin leader is planning a drone attack on a NATO member state.
Former Tory defence minister and former Army captain Tobias Ellwood said the sharp rise in drone incidents detected in the UK suggests that the UK Armed Forces are being viewed "as a target". He added that the government is "asleep" to such threats.
Quote from Ellwood: "Here in the UK we are doing nothing about protecting our critical national infrastructure, as well as military bases, and it's such an easy way to disrupt.
At the moment these are just rogue drones, and they're passive, but it's not a huge step to then add a kinetic dimension to them to make them introduce lethality. All this points to the fact that we are not taking the rise in threat levels that our European cousins are addressing seriously at all."
Background:
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, citing intelligence data, that Russia is planning hybrid attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.
- Kęstutis Budrys, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Lithuania, confirmed that his country also possesses intelligence about Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies after a similar warning from Donald Tusk.

articles.title: Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure
articles.body:
Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure
Former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
He noted that Ukraine has significantly increased its drone production during the years of the full-scale war, from several thousand to nearly 10 million annually. In the politician’s view, further scaling up these capabilities, combined with the development of missile systems, could fundamentally shift the balance of power.
Landsbergis stressed that building a comprehensive deterrence system requires not only weapons themselves but also the necessary infrastructure, including guidance systems and satellite capabilities.
“Add ballistic missiles to that. Good guidance systems, satellites and the like are also needed – to reach the point where, with or without allies, Ukraine can tell Putin: ‘Look, even if you try again next time, you will have no industry left,’” the politician said.
He believes Ukraine is uniquely positioned to establish such a system and that Western countries can help it achieve this.
“There is no other country that could do this – only Ukraine. And we, the West, are capable of helping Ukraine achieve it,” Landsbergis said.
At the same time, he believes Ukraine’s experience could also be used to strengthen the defenses of other countries potentially threatened by Russia.
Lithuania and other neighboring countries of Russia, in particular, could develop their own long-range deterrence systems adapted to their capabilities. According to the politician, this would allow countries in the region to rely not only on assistance from their allies but also on their own capabilities.
“That is what deterrence is – sovereign power,” Landsbergis emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 18, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced during his visit to Ukraine that Poland had joined the Antiballistic Coalition.

articles.title: Russia reports ‘powerful’ cyberattacks on second day of parliamentary vote
articles.body:
Russia reports ‘powerful’ cyberattacks on second day of parliamentary vote
This is Russia’s first election since it invaded Ukraine, and is expected to gauge public support for the ongoing war.
Russian authorities have reported attacks on the country’s voting systems and communication lines on the second day of a tightly controlled three-day-long parliamentary election.
Moscow’s electronic voting system was subjected to a powerful cyberattack overnight between Friday and Saturday, and the attack has continued, Interfax news agency reported.
Recommended Stories

- list 4 of 4Russia kills eight people in Ukraine, attacks two vessels in Black Sea
“The Moscow system was under a very powerful attack, literally non-stop, all night long,” Ella Pamfilova, head of the Russian Central Election Commission, told reporters on Saturday morning. “This attack is ongoing almost constantly, and it’s very large-scale and intense, meaning it’s currently targeting Moscow.”
Pamfilova said the electronic voting system is still operating as normal, and did not give details on the nature of the attack or who was responsible.
The election, which will decide all 450 seats in Russia’s lower house, the State Duma, is due to run until 18:00 GMT on Sunday.
The State Duma election is the first since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022, and is widely expected to see the governing pro-Putin United Russia party maintain its dominance in Russia’s tightly controlled political system.
Most antiwar candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia’s 11 time zones got under way, after the Supreme Court ruled last month that the liberal Yabloko party – which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine – had breached electoral rules, which it has denied.
Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Ukraine on Friday of trying to “hinder” the vote, an accusation to which Kyiv has not responded. Ukraine has called the election farcical.
More than 350 Ukrainian drones targeted the Russian capital on Friday morning, Moscow’s mayor reported.
With the vote potentially offering the Kremlin a measure of the public mood over the invasion, Kyiv has maintained its bid to use air attacks to make Russians feel the impact of the conflict politically, socially, and economically.
Nationwide turnout as of 14:00 local time on Saturday (11:00 GMT) stood at 32.58 percent, according to CEC data cited by state media.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that Russians are showing active participation in the ongoing State Duma elections despite physical threats and cyber challenges. She said that the high voter turnout shows people’s united response to the war declared against Russia and its people.

articles.title: Israel seeks ‘compensation’ from US following Saudi F-35 deal: Report
articles.body:
Khaled Yousef and Serdar Dincel
19 September 2026•Update: 19 September 2026
Israel plans to ask for US additional defense capabilities as a "compensation" after Washington agreed to sell F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, according to Israeli media.
Tel Aviv will seek to purchase weapons systems that US President Donald Trump's administration had previously declined to approve, Israeli news website Walla reported on Friday.
Israel’s military focus extends beyond advanced fighter jets and next-generation stealth aircraft to space-based weapons and the development and production of interceptor aircraft, the outlet said.
Weapons to be demanded by Israeli officials also include "bunker-busting munitions and underground systems capable of operating deep beneath rocky mountains,” it added.
The move is intended to secure a “compensation” from Washington following the F-35 deal with Riyadh, the website said.
On Thursday, the US State Department approved a possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.
The package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, along with cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, training and logistics packages, according to a notification sent to the US Congress.
If completed, the deal would make Saudi Arabia the first Arab country to acquire F-35 fighter jets, while Israel is currently the only operator of the aircraft in the Middle East.
Israeli officials have repeatedly criticized Saudi Arabia over its refusal to normalize relations with Tel Aviv before the establishment of a Palestinian state along the 1967 borders, a condition which the international community supports while Israel continues to reject.

He said the first operation targeted “sensitive targets” in Riyadh, while the second targeted Saudi Aramco in the western coastal city of Yanbu.

On July 20, the Houthis announced what they called a “maritime blockade” on Saudi Arabia before later claiming missile and drone attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and sites.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since March 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.

articles.title: Russia reportedly buries its drone factory underground
articles.body:
- Ukrainian analyst Dnipro Osint said Russia has built about 42,000 square meters of underground production space for Shahed/Geran drones at Alabuga.
- The claim follows confirmed satellite evidence of new production halls, a 340-hectare site expansion, and defensive towers built around the facility in 2026.
Russia has begun building underground production space for its Shahed and Geran attack drones at the Alabuga industrial zone in Tatarstan, according to Ukrainian open-source intelligence analyst Dnipro Osint, who estimated roughly 42,000 square meters of underground area has already been constructed there.
Dnipro Osint said the shift underground appears to have followed earlier Ukrainian strikes on the Alabuga site, and that Russia has been expanding the underground infrastructure quickly since then.
The analyst placed the activity at coordinates 55.808719°, 52.026664°, within the broader Alabuga Special Economic Zone near the city of Yelabuga, roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) from the Ukrainian border. This specific underground construction claim comes from a single open-source analyst and has not yet been independently confirmed through separate satellite imagery analysis.
Alabuga is Russia’s primary production site for the Geran-2, a Russian-built version of Iran’s Shahed-136 one-way attack drone that Russian forces fire at Ukrainian cities on a near-nightly basis. The facility has grown substantially over the past year. Satellite imagery cited by Radio Liberty showed the zone’s footprint expanded by 340 hectares between May 2025 and May 2026, with new hangars, dormitories for foreign workers, and a roughly 450-hectare construction area added south of the M-12 highway. Ukrainian analysts reported on Sept. 14 that five additional production halls had gone up in the southern part of the site, based on satellite images similarly sourced from Dnipro Osint.
Russia has also added physical protection around the plant. Satellite images from July and August analyzed by Spencer Faragasso of the Institute for Science and International Security showed a two-ring system of lattice towers under construction around Alabuga’s production buildings, an arrangement meant to complicate future drone or missile strikes on the site.
Dnipro Osint said the combined effect of these changes, underground construction, dispersed production buildings and added physical defenses, is making Russia’s drone manufacturing base progressively harder and more expensive to target. The site relies heavily on foreign labor recruited through the Alabuga Polytechnic College and other channels; the United Kingdom sanctioned 35 entities and individuals in May 2026 over recruitment tied to the facility, and the site remains under separate U.S. and European Union sanctions.

articles.title: Russia’s next-gen Armata tank remains stuck a decade after debut
articles.body:
- New dashcam footage this week showed a Russian T-14 Armata tank crossing toward a firing range, with no new program details released.
- Russia has built roughly 20 T-14s against an original 2,300-tank target, and continues to rely on upgraded T-90M tanks for the war in Ukraine.
New dashcam footage circulating on Russian state-aligned media this week shows a T-14 Armata tank crossing a dirt road toward a firing range, the latest glimpse of a next-generation tank program that has spent a decade struggling to move beyond testing.
No new technical details accompanied the footage, and it does not appear to show anything beyond a routine range exercise. The clip, recorded from a passing civilian vehicle’s dashcam, adds to a long pattern of brief, unofficial sightings that have periodically resurfaced online since the T-14 was first unveiled during rehearsals for Russia’s 2015 Victory Day parade.
The T-14 represented a sharp break from Soviet-era tank design when Uralvagonzavod introduced it, built around an unmanned turret, a separately armored crew capsule, and the Afghanit active protection system meant to intercept incoming projectiles before they hit the vehicle. Russia originally planned to build more than 2,300 of the tanks by 2020. A decade later, estimates put the actual number built at roughly 20, most of them prototypes or pre-production vehicles rather than a true production run.
Cost has been the central obstacle. Estimates for the T-14 range from about $8 million to $15 million per vehicle, compared with $1.5 million to $2.5 million for an upgraded T-90M, the tank Russia has relied on instead throughout its war in Ukraine. Despite repeated claims from Russian officials and pro-government media that the T-14 has seen combat, no independently verified evidence has emerged confirming it ever fought at the front. Russian media reported in mid-2023 that a small number of Armatas reached Ukraine and fired from standoff range before being withdrawn within months, but outside analysts were never able to confirm those claims. British defense intelligence assessed at the time that Russian troops were reluctant to accept the tanks into service and that any deployment would likely serve propaganda purposes rather than combat need.
Even Rostec, the state conglomerate that oversees the T-14’s development, has acknowledged the program’s limits. Rostec chief executive Sergey Chemezov told Russian state news agency in March 2024 that while the Armata outperformed everything else in Russia’s inventory, it was too expensive to field at scale, and that the war would instead be fought with upgraded T-90Ms and refurbished T-72s. Uralvagonzavod, the world’s largest tank plant and the T-14’s manufacturer, has since turned much of its production capacity toward exactly that work, rebuilding older T-72 hulls and building new T-90Ms rather than expanding Armata output.
Some Russian defense industry figures have floated a different path forward, arguing that individual technologies developed for the T-14, its firepower, protection or mobility systems, could be transferred into the more widely fielded T-90M and T-72 rather than fielding the Armata itself in large numbers. Russia has also offered to transfer T-14 technology to India for local production under that country’s domestic manufacturing program, though that arrangement has not produced any confirmed manufacturing to date.
Analysts who track the program have grown increasingly skeptical of its future. Long development timelines and design choices that outside experts say have not kept pace with battlefield lessons from Ukraine have led some to describe the Armata as functionally dead on arrival as a mass-production tank, even as isolated footage like this week’s clip keeps the program in public view.

articles.title: USA to Sell Ukraine S-300 Clone Missiles
articles.body:
The United States has approved the sale of S-300 Clone missiles to Ukraine as part of a new package of equipment and weapons.
Apart from a mention in the U.S. State Department’s list, no further information about these missiles has been provided.
Their purchase will be financed by European partners and through funds from the U.S. Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program.
The then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin first spoke about work on new missiles for the air defense system back in September 2024.
At a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in Ramstein, he announced joint work with Ukraine on developing a ‘replacement’ for the Soviet S-300 air defense systems and R-27 air-to-air missiles.
“With the support of several European companies, the United States is working with Ukraine to develop and manufacture a replacement for the S-300 surface-to-air missile system, as well as the R-27 air-to-air missile,” Austin said.
In August 2026, Robert Hamilton, a retired U.S. Army colonel and president of the Delphi Global Research Center, spoke about the joint development of new missiles.
According to him, the project involves the production of 100–200 anti-aircraft missiles per year.
In addition to work on developing missiles in collaboration with partners, there are also reports of localization efforts in Ukraine. Localization involves bringing European partners on board the project.
Prior to the start of the Russian invasion in 2022, Ukraine had approximately 25–30 battalions of S-300PT/PS systems at its disposal, in varying states of operational readiness.
The systems currently deployed in Ukraine are designed to counter strategic and tactical aircraft, as well as cruise missiles, at altitudes ranging from 25 m to 27 km and at ranges of up to 100 km.
On April 8, 2022, the then-Prime Minister of Slovakia, Eduard Heger, announced the provision of an additional S-300PMU air defense system to Ukraine, which had been in service with his country.
During combat operations, certain components (launchers and radars) were lost, and Ukraine’s missile stockpiles were depleted. For this reason, partners—including Norway—allocated funds for Ukraine to purchase missiles from third countries. However, a shortage persists.

articles.title: Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
articles.body:
Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
The far-right parties the White House favors have a foreign-policy agenda that won’t serve American interests.
Donald Trump says he wants a Europe that is more capable of defending itself. But the nationalist-populist movements he is championing there will not advance this agenda and may put Europe at odds with the United States over China.
Earlier this month, the nationalist-populist Alternative for Germany party came just a few seats short of an outright majority in a regional parliament, its best-ever result. This Sunday, Germans will vote in two more regional elections. The ruling Christian Democrats are behind in both races, and the AfD is expected to do well in one. On Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled his visit to the United Nations General Assembly next week, sparking speculation that he could soon be forced to resign.
U.S. officials are ebullient. Trump greeted the AfD’s recent electoral victory with a triumphant message on Truth Social that finished with “MGGA” (Make Germany Great Again). Richard Grenell, Trump’s former ambassador to Germany and now a presidential envoy, called the result “a huge win and a new day in Germany.”
The Trump administration has consistently embraced Europe’s nationalist-populist parties as ideological partners, and even launched a State Department fund to support MAGA-aligned European groups. It surely sees the AfD’s ascendance as a sign that politics are moving in its direction. But that is true only if Trump’s real goal is a fragmented Europe that accommodates Russian and Chinese power and is unable to punch its weight. Such an outcome would be catastrophic for U.S. interests.
Some people in the administration insist that the idea is not to weaken Europe but to shift the burden for its conventional defense to the Europeans themselves. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for example, reject claims that the administration is soft on Russia and say that they are calling instead for greater European self-sufficiency. Colby advocates for what he calls NATO 3.0, in which Europeans would take on the primary responsibility for their conventional defense.
But the nationalist populists do not share this view. The AfD has called for an end to all arms deliveries to Ukraine and a lifting of all sanctions on Russia. Its co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, boycotted Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the Bundestag in 2024, dismissing the Ukrainian president as a “war and beggar president.”
In France, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the nationalist-populist party National Rally and the front-runner for next spring’s presidential election, has promised to take France out of NATO’s integrated military command (France would remain a member of the alliance). Such a withdrawal would hardly help the Trump administration shift the burden of NATO’s defense to Europe.
The Trump administration’s affinity for Europe’s nationalist-populist right seems to be almost entirely cultural and civilizational, and based on the notion that Europe’s populists are fighting the same culture wars—including against immigration—as their counterparts in the United States. J. D. Vance explicitly praised then–Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as an ally in defense of Western civilization at an election rally in Budapest on the eve of the Hungarian elections. And the Trump team seems to see the European populist right’s enemies—the European Union and national political establishments—as versions of its own domestic foes. This commonality appears to take precedence over foreign-policy concerns.
Trump officials have blasted centrist European governments for being too soft on Beijing but have said nothing about the populist right’s position on China. Some of these parties—particularly the AfD and Fidesz, in Hungary—favor much closer ties to the American adversary. The AfD’s Weidel lived in China for six years, speaks Mandarin, and wrote her doctoral dissertation about China’s pension system. Chrupalla, her co-leader, accused the German government of waging “economic war” against China for proposing a tougher trade policy toward Beijing. They have both called for warmer relations with China. Orbán, who was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, blocked the EU from criticizing Beijing, initiated an “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership” with China, and welcomed Chinese investment in Hungarian infrastructure.
These largely transactional attitudes toward China and Russia may reflect a broader worldview among the nationalist populists, who praise Trump but are deeply skeptical of American power. In an analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Jeremy Cliffe argued that the AfD supports a multipolar world order and believes that great powers, such as China and Russia, should possess spheres of influence—a perspective that Trump seems sympathetic toward. The AfD, Cliffe wrote, “may regard Trump as a civilizational ally, but its senior figures have long described the United States as a raumfremd in Europe, a hard to translate German word that means something like ‘territorially alien.’”
If parties with these views take power, they could reduce American influence in Europe while making common European action on Russia and China much more difficult. They will also make Eastern Europeans nervous about German rearmament. In 2011, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, said, “I fear German power less than German inaction.” He recently revisited that remark, telling the German newspaper Handelsblatt, “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as the largest economy in Europe, to play a strong role in securing our common security. But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany can lead in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party—and that is exactly what the AfD represents.”
Senior Trump-administration officials say they are building a Europe that will carry its own weight. Maybe they are so beguiled by the nationalist populists’ domestic agenda that they have not yet realized it will come at the expense of NATO 3.0. Or maybe Trump doesn’t care about Europe’s defense, doesn’t see it as a U.S. interest, and doesn’t believe that Europe has any contribution to make to America’s security.
Trump and Vance seem to be laying the foundation for a more divided Europe that is incapable of deterring Russia, ever more dependent on China, and at odds with itself. If the administration continues on this path, it may get the European culture war it wants, but the United States will lose its ally.

articles.title: Israel demands 'compensation' from US after Saudi F-35 sale

US officials said this week they are planning to deliver tens of thousands of heavy 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal.
Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region have long sought to purchase F-35s, which are advanced fifth-generation stealth fighters.

articles.title: Britain deepens nuclear ties with France and Australia
articles.body:
Britain is deepening its nuclear relationships with the United States, France and Australia, with the Northwood Declaration recognising that there is no extreme threat to Europe which would not prompt a response by both Britain and France, according to the annual update to Parliament published this week.
The declaration, agreed in July 2025, reaffirmed and strengthened what the update describes as longstanding nuclear cooperation between the two countries. On the AUKUS partnership, the update records an important development in February this year when HMS Anson docked at HMAS Stirling near Perth.
The United States is described as Britain’s closest defence ally, with the relationship underpinned by long-standing cooperation on all nuclear matters including policy, operations and technology.
The practical expression of that relationship runs through the missile system, since Trident and its supporting systems fitted to the Vanguard class are manufactured in the United States, with Britain having bought title to a number of missiles drawn from a shared pool of assets under the 1963 Polaris Sales Agreement as amended for Trident in 1982. The system is operated independently by both the Royal Navy and the United States Navy.
The warhead fitted to those missiles is sovereign to Britain, with the Mk4A design maintained by AWE at Aldermaston, which also leads development of the replacement warhead, Astraea. Wes Streeting writes that the increase in investment across the enterprise “sends a clear signal of our commitment to global security, and to our Allies”, with the deterrent remaining declared to the defence of NATO.
The update states that nuclear deterrence is the cornerstone of NATO security and that the independent strategic nuclear forces of the United Kingdom contribute significantly to the overall security of the alliance, a declaration maintained since 1962.

articles.title: Trump Signs Lindsey Graham Bill Imposing Tariffs of Up to 100% on Buyers of Russian Oil
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump signed a law that expands sanctions against Russia and allows for tariffs of up to 100% to be imposed on the largest buyers of Russian energy resources.
This was announced by the White House.
The bill is named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of the initiators of increased sanctions pressure on Russia.
The law allows for tariffs of up to 100% to be imposed on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas.
The bill also provides for sanctions against Russian officials, financial institutions, and other individuals associated with the Russian government. Certain provisions are aimed at preventing circumvention of existing restrictions.
In addition, the law extends sanctions against Iran. The inclusion of these provisions was previously supported by the Donald Trump administration.
On September 16, the bill was approved by the U.S. House of Representatives, after which it was sent to the president for his signature. Prior to that, on August 7, the Senate had passed it.
As reported by Militarnyi, the Senate passed the bill by a vote of 86 to 11. The final version differs significantly from the original bill proposed by Lindsey Graham.
Initially, the bill proposed imposing tariffs of up to 500% on countries purchasing Russian oil, gas, and other goods.
In the final version, the maximum rate was lowered to 100%, and the application of these tariffs was focused on the five largest importers of Russian oil and the five largest importers of natural gas.
While he was still alive, Graham explained the necessity of the bill by noting that purchases of Russian energy resources provide Moscow with revenue that it can use to finance the war against Ukraine. Among the largest buyers of Russian oil, he specifically mentioned China and India.
At the same time, the law grants the U.S. president considerable discretion in applying the measures it provides for, particularly regarding exemptions and the lifting of sanctions once a peace agreement is reached.

articles.title: New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
articles.body:
New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
The major US sanctions law signed by President Donald Trump this week will undermine efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
On Friday, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorizes tougher restrictions on Moscow and tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“Clearly, this cannot have a positive effect,” Peskov told RIA Novosti on Saturday when asked how the law would affect prospects for a peaceful settlement in Ukraine and a possible “breakthrough” in Russian-US relations.
Named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who co-authored the original bill with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal in 2025, the legislation remained stalled for months as Trump pursued diplomacy with Russia and resisted placing sole blame for the conflict on Moscow. Trump’s envoys also discussed normalizing economic ties with their Russian counterparts.
The Senate passed the measure 86-11 last month, followed by the House on Wednesday in a 262-159 vote.
The original proposal threatened tariffs of 500% on countries purchasing Russian energy, but the maximum rate was reduced to 100% after negotiations with the White House. Graham, who died unexpectedly in July, had promoted the measure as “sanctions from hell” intended to deliver a “bone-crushing” blow to Moscow.
The version adopted by Congress targets major buyers of Russian oil and gas, with China and India expected to be among those potentially affected. It also gives Trump broad discretion over the application of the tariffs, including the ability to waive or suspend restrictions in the national interest.
Peskov previously described the bill as an “unfriendly action” that would “complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in the US said the legislation had done “a grand disservice” to Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, arguing that restricting Russian energy trade amid sharply reduced Middle Eastern supplies could send fuel prices soaring ahead of the midterm elections. It warned that confrontation with Russia and China would be a “lose-lose situation” benefiting only “Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun also condemned the new law, saying that China “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit” and that its trade was not directed against any third country.

articles.title: Britain exploring return to making its own reactor fuel
articles.body:
Britain has begun exploring options to re-establish the production of reactor fuel for defence purposes, work the government says would be fully consistent with its obligations under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, according to the annual update to Parliament published this week.
The Nuclear Fuels Programme is part of the recapitalisation the Defence Nuclear Enterprise is carrying out simultaneously, which the update describes as covering two submarine build programmes with a further one in design, two warhead programmes, the fuel cycle work, and the infrastructure required to build and maintain those capabilities.
Every British submarine is nuclear powered, with the reactors manufactured by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Raynesway near Derby. The update describes nuclear propulsion as critical to sustaining continuous at sea deterrence, allowing submarines to remain dived on long-range patrols without detection.
Raynesway is one of the two sites receiving a share of the £6 billion committed under the Defence Investment Plan for infrastructure, alongside Barrow-in-Furness, investment the update says will grow the capability of the enterprise to produce a submarine every eighteen months in future.
Britain last enriched uranium for defence purposes at Capenhurst, and the country has relied on existing stocks for reactor fuel since domestic production ceased, which is the position the exploration now under way would change.
The update sets out the rest of the submarine picture alongside it. The Royal Navy has operated the Vanguard class since 1993, and those boats will be replaced by the Dreadnought class, with steel cut for the fourth and final Dreadnought in September 2025 on the same day the King commissioned HMS Agamemnon, the sixth Astute-class submarine.
The Astute class supports the deterrent while also undertaking other defence and intelligence tasks, including work with maritime task groups. Beyond those two programmes sits SSN-AUKUS, the design now in progress, with BAE Systems, the Defence Nuclear Organisation, Babcock and Rolls-Royce Submarines all maintaining teams at Barrow contributing to it.
The enterprise spent £12 billion in the 2025/26 financial year and projects spend of over £100 billion through British suppliers over the next ten years, with in excess of £20 billion more going into it between 2026/27 and 2029/30 than across the previous four years.

The UK Ministry of Defence did not provide details about whom it suspects of being behind the incidents. However, experts say hostile actors operating on behalf of Moscow or Tehran could be responsible.
Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative defence minister and former military officer, said the sharp increase in recorded drone incidents suggests that the British armed forces are being regarded "as a target." He added that the government is "asleep" to such threats.
"At the moment these are just rogue drones, and they're passive, but it's not a huge step to then add a kinetic dimension to them to make them introduce lethality. All this points to the fact that we are not taking the rise in threat levels that our European cousins are addressing seriously at all," he said.
Ellwood said Russia and Iran are "100 percent" responsible for many of these incidents.
"They are absolutely active in Britain in plotting, mapping, and then recruiting useful idiots to prosecute this targeting. It could be criminal gangs as well, but they would then be supported by Russia. Russia is by far the obvious culprit here... It's not China's style. They tend to do things in a different way," he said.
At the same time, the UK Ministry of Defence said the increase in recorded incidents reflects improvements in reporting systems, better drone-detection technology, and greater awareness among military personnel.
Minister for the Armed Forces Louise Sanderson-Jones told The Independent that the government is extremely serious about the threat posed by hostile drones to defence sites. She said the authorities are investing in counter-drone systems and giving military personnel new powers to disable drones that threaten defence facilities.
"In February, we established new restricted airspace areas over 44 critical defence sites in the UK. This autumn, we will introduce restricted airspace areas over a further 160 sites," she said. "By the end of the year, the Armed Forces Bill will become law, giving our personnel the power to take out drones – whether in the air, on the ground, or in the water – posing a threat to any defence site without the need for assistance from the police."
She also said that since taking office, the government has quadrupled spending on counter-drone capabilities. Under the Defence Investment Plan, GBP 750 million has been allocated to counter-drone systems and to protecting the British armed forces both within the UK and while deployed overseas.
As Ukrinform reported, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the Royal Navy, Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said that Russia is "testing Britain's vulnerabilities" and could attempt to damage the country's transatlantic cables on the first day of a conflict.

US President Donald Trump has criticized Seoul in recent weeks over what he described as a lack of South Korean support for US efforts to pressure Iran. The two countries have also yet to finalise agreements governing $350 billion in South Korean investments pledged under a trade deal reached last year.
Cho explained to Rubio Seoul's willingness to make a substantive contribution to restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, the ministry said in a statement without elaborating.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is due in the United States next week for the UN General Assembly, said on Friday he would not deploy military assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict.
However, he said Seoul was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
Cho said before leaving Seoul on Thursday that investment plans under its trade deal had been delayed while procedural issues were clarified, without elaborating.

articles.title: From My Lai to Minab: A question every American should ask themselves
articles.body:
From My Lai to Minab: A question every American should ask themselves
TEHRAN — After the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it had reasonable grounds to believe that the United States had committed war crimes in two attacks — on a school in Minab and a sports stadium in Lamerd — during its military assault on Iran, Washington responded with a hasty denial, offering no evidence to substantiate its rejection of the findings.
The denial came as a Bloomberg investigation reported that, within hours of a U.S. missile strike on an elementary school in Minab that killed more than 120 children, some Pentagon personnel already knew that American missiles had caused the massacre.
Some may wonder how the U.S. government can deny such blatant crimes. Let us travel back in time, several decades.
On the morning of March 16, 1968, U.S. troops entered the Sơn Mỹ village complex in South Vietnam’s Quảng Ngãi Province. One of the areas was known as My Lai. American forces expected to encounter Viet Cong fighters, but instead found themselves among a civilian population. Nevertheless, troops from a U.S. unit carried out a mass killing of civilians, slaughtering around 500 people.
The U.S. military covered up a crime of such magnitude, and for nearly a year there was little public knowledge of what had happened. It took a year before the disclosures of a former soldier, Ronald Ridenhour, followed by the investigative reporting of Seymour Hersh, shed light on the shocking episode and brought it to public attention.
Investigations showed that the crime was not simply the product of a collective breakdown or madness within a single military unit on the battlefield. The chain of command — and, beyond it, the political and senior leadership responsible for managing the war — bore responsibility for what had happened.
In cases like this, there is a natural tendency to point the finger at the person who pulled the trigger and put that individual in the dock. But limiting responsibility to the soldiers who ultimately pull the trigger is itself where the problem begins.
The My Lai massacre was horrific enough to awaken any political system — and, more importantly, any society. But that did not happen in America.
Two years ago, around this very time, The New Yorker published a thought-provoking investigation into the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the September 11 attacks. Titled “The War Crimes That the Military Buried,” the report was the product of four years of investigation.It found that the U.S. military had committed around 800 war crimes in the two wars, that only a small number of these cases had been prosecuted, and that an even smaller number had resulted in convictions. 
 
 The question of whether such a small number of convictions bears any reasonable proportion to the number of war crimes committed is a matter worthy of serious consideration in its own right.
Some would like to attribute the recent chaos and the crimes committed entirely to Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth, creating the impression that the storm will subside once they are gone. This view is less a reflection of reality than an oversimplification — and a sanitization — of America’s history of war crimes.
War crimes are a recurring feature of American history, and Democratic and Republican administrations have had a remarkably similar record in this regard. The problem runs deeper than the narcissism and authoritarian tendencies attributed to Trump, or Hegseth’s attitudes and approaches that critics have described as irrational.
The American people, as those who elect their governments, should ask themselves serious and difficult questions.
What is their responsibility for these crimes?
From senior political leaders to the architects and commanders of elective and criminal wars, and those who ultimately pulled the triggers or pressed the buttons to launch missiles and release bombs, none of these people came from another planet.
Will Americans continue to measure the cost of war not in lives lost and crimes committed, but in the price displayed at the pump?
Iranians have a well-known proverb: "The world is round" — meaning what goes around comes around. History has a way of settling its accounts.

articles.title: Lockheed gets $76.6M for next-gen of Trident II nuclear missile
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $76.6 million contract modification for continued design work on the next-generation Trident II D5LE2 nuclear missile.
- The program aims to keep the submarine-launched missile in service through roughly 2084, arming the future Columbia-class and Dreadnought-class submarines.
The U.S. Navy has added $76.6 million to a Lockheed Martin contract for continued design work on the next generation of the Trident II D5 nuclear missile, part of a long-term effort meant to keep the submarine-launched weapon in service into the 2080s.
The modification adds to an existing contract with Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office that manages the country’s submarine-launched nuclear deterrent, and covers advanced design and development work under the Trident II D5 Life Extension 2 program, known as D5LE2. Lockheed Martin’s Titusville, Florida division will lead the effort, though the work itself is spread across more than a dozen locations, with Denver, Colorado handling 51 percent, followed by smaller shares in Elkton, Maryland; Montville, New Jersey; Greeneville, Tennessee; and Cape Canaveral, Florida, among others. The Navy is obligating the full $76.6 million now from fiscal 2026 weapons procurement funds, with work scheduled to run through Sept. 30, 2030. The award was not competitively bid, a legal option the Navy can use for specialized defense work, and only one company submitted a proposal after the opportunity was posted publicly.
Trident II D5 missiles form the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad, the three-part system of submarines, land-based missiles and bomber aircraft that has underpinned American nuclear deterrence for decades. The missile first entered service in 1990 and went through its first major refresh, called D5LE, in 2017. This second life extension effort is meant to keep the weapon effective for decades beyond that, with the Navy targeting continued service through roughly 2084, nearly a century after the missile’s original design.
The current Trident II D5 weighs about 130,000 pounds (59,000 kilograms), can fly roughly 4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km), and reaches speeds reported to exceed Mach 20. It currently arms the Navy’s Ohio-class submarines and Britain’s Royal Navy Vanguard-class boats, both of which are approaching retirement. The D5LE2 version being developed now is intended to carry over onto the submarines replacing them, the Navy’s incoming Columbia-class and the Royal Navy’s future Dreadnought-class, making this a joint U.S.-U.K. modernization effort rather than a purely American one.
The program has moved forward in stages. The Navy first awarded Lockheed a $383 million contract in January 2025 to begin D5LE2 design and development, followed by an $850 million contract modification announced in April 2026 to continue that work. Lockheed is separately building a roughly 225,000-square-foot (20,900-square-meter) production facility in Titusville expected to open in 2027, while the Navy is constructing its own 130,000-square-foot Engineering Test Facility at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, one of 28 facility projects the Naval Ordnance Test Unit plans to complete between 2024 and 2032 to support the missile’s development and testing.
Even as the newer version moves through design work, the current fleet of missiles remains active. The Navy conducted four unarmed Trident II D5LE test flights from an Ohio-class submarine off the coast of Florida in September 2025, a demonstration officials said confirmed the continued readiness of the sea-based deterrent while the next generation is still years from completion.
